frameworks.name: Start-Stop-Keep Feedback Format
frameworks.definition: A three-part feedback structure: identify behaviors you want someone to start (not currently doing), stop (currently doing but unwanted), and keep (currently doing and valuable). Translates culture into observable behavioral directives.

frameworks.name: Culture-Talent-Training Execution Triad
frameworks.definition: Three-part diagnostic for why execution fails: (1) Culture — the rules governing what gets rewarded and punished; (2) Talent — the quality of people doing the behaviors; (3) Training — translating abstract goals into observable, repeatable behaviors.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that plan conviction matters more than plan perfection for business success: most people have a sufficiently good strategy, and the binding constraint is executing and sticking with that strategy rather than identifying a better one.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Applies across business stages from early-stage through $5M+ revenue
claims.mechanism: Switching paths requires returning to the base level and starting the climb again, wasting accumulated context and momentum; execution skill compounds on a single path but resets at zero with each switch.
bounded_by: Does not apply when the strategy is fundamentally flawed (dull knife metaphor)

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that anyone willing to persistently attempt a skill for 100 consecutive days can outperform the majority of competitors in that skill, because most competitors quit at the first sign of difficulty before reaching competency.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: willing to suck at something for a hundred days in a row
conditions: Consistent daily effort over the 100-day period
Applies to most business and professional skills
claims.mechanism: The majority of competitors quit when they encounter their first unknown or difficulty; enduring through the uncertainty phase is rare, making persistence itself the differentiating factor rather than talent or intelligence.

numbers.axis: days of persistent practice before competitive advantage materializes

anchors.value: quit at first sign of difficulty
100 days of consistent effort beats most people

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that operating nine businesses simultaneously at CEO level produced near-zero net income despite generating revenue, because insufficient focus prevented effective execution in any single business — illustrating that spread attention compounds revenue without compounding profit.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Applies when founder is simultaneously CEO of multiple operationally demanding businesses
Revenue was present; profitability was the constraint
claims.mechanism: Attention spread across nine businesses meant no single business received enough founder focus to compound; each business hovered at survival level rather than growth level.

numbers.axis: number of simultaneous businesses vs. outcome

anchors.value: revenue without profit — barely keeping head above water

claims.text: Alex Hormozi defines business culture as the rules of reinforcement that govern which behaviors get rewarded and which get punished; culture is not a vibe or set of values, but the observable pattern of what is allowed to persist in an organization.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that culture is transmitted through two primary signals: who leadership hires and fires, and which behaviors leadership allows to continue unremarked. Permitting a behavior without consequence teaches the team that behavior is acceptable.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: who you hire and who you fire
claims.mechanism: If someone shows up late and nothing is said, the team infers lateness is acceptable; if someone performs well and receives no reward, they infer that performance is not valued. Silence is itself a reinforcement signal.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that paying for 90th-percentile talent (approximately $115,000/year for a role whose 50th-percentile salary is $75,000/year) is a favorable investment because the top performer is roughly five times more effective than the median performer while costing only about 30% more.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Assumes a role where performance variability is high (e.g., sales, creative, product)
Based on Hormozi's own operational experience, not a controlled study
claims.mechanism: Top-percentile talent compounds output multiplicatively rather than additively; paying 30% above median to get 5x effectiveness is a positive-ROI trade.

numbers.axis: annual salary vs. relative effectiveness for a given role

bounded_by: Effectiveness multiplier is Hormozi's estimate, not a controlled measurement
May not apply to highly commoditized roles where performance variance is low

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that using generic abstract terms like 'accountability' in training produces zero behavior change, because different people hold different mental models of what the term means; translating abstract concepts into specific observable micro-behaviors is required for consistent execution.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: we have to translate these big words into smaller actions
conditions: Applies to any organizational training or culture-setting effort where abstract values are used
Validated against a solar sales company's failed two-day leadership offsite
claims.mechanism: When two parties share a word but not its referent, each person believes they are complying while executing different behaviors; feedback loops break because there is no shared observable criterion for success or failure.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that interviewing candidates about their off-hours activities reliably predicts full-time work quality: a candidate whose discretionary time is spent practicing the target skill will produce higher output and accept improvement feedback more readily than one whose off-hours are unrelated to the role.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Applies to roles where intrinsic skill obsession compounds performance (creative, sales, technical)
Hiring signal, not a guarantee — used as a screening filter, not a sole criterion
claims.mechanism: A candidate who spends discretionary effort on the same skill needed in the role is already engaging in non-compensated improvement; their intrinsic motivation compounds performance beyond what compensation alone can produce. A candidate moonlighting to another passion will always allocate their best discretionary effort there.
bounded_by: Does not apply to roles where performance is independent of intrinsic interest (repetitive process roles)
Self-reported off-hours activity may not accurately reflect actual behavior

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that intelligence is preferable to domain experience when hiring for lower-level roles, because a high-intelligence low-experience candidate will rapidly close the experience gap and then surpass a less-intelligent but more-experienced candidate.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: smart person will be able to catch up to that dumber person really quickly and then pass them
conditions: Applies to lower-level roles in the organizational hierarchy where learning speed matters more than immediate output
At senior levels, the preference reverses: actual demonstrated ability matters more than potential
claims.mechanism: Intelligence operationalized as learning rate means a fast learner compresses months of experience into weeks; experience advantage of a slower learner erodes and then reverses over time.
bounded_by: Does not apply to senior roles where the gap between potential and actual performance is too costly to absorb
Does not apply in regulated roles requiring certified experience (medicine, law, engineering)

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that the difficulty of not knowing what to do — the uncertainty phase — is the primary point at which most businesspeople fail and switch strategies, not the difficulty of the work itself; misattributing uncertainty as a strategy problem leads to perpetual path-switching instead of problem-solving.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: the not knowing part is the part that's hard
conditions: Based on Hormozi's observations from coaching and consulting business owners at multiple revenue stages
claims.mechanism: When a path becomes uncertain (unknown next steps), the existing path feels more costly than it is and a new path looks appealing because its hidden costs are invisible. This leads founders to restart at zero rather than solve the present constraint.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that switching strategies when stuck causes compounding effort loss because the builder must descend to the base of the new path before ascending again, wasting all progress made; in contrast, solving the current constraint on the existing path compounds all prior progress.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: you have to go back down and then you got to go over and then you got to go up again
claims.mechanism: Progress on any path includes accumulated context, relationships, process knowledge, and reputation that cannot transfer to a new path; switching resets these to zero.
bounded_by: Does not apply when the core strategy is demonstrably broken (e.g., no market demand, illegal, wrong unit economics)

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that the three root causes of failed business execution are diagnosable as distinct failures — culture (wrong reinforcement rules), talent (insufficient people quality), or training (abstract goals not translated into observable behaviors) — and prescribes distinct remedies for each rather than a general strategy change.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Assumes the strategy itself is sensible
Applies when a business has revenue but is not executing its plan consistently

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that most people can outperform 99% of competitors without superior intelligence or luck by being willing to endure pain and uncertainty for longer than competitors will, because the competitive bar for sustained effort has never been lower.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: beat 99% of people without being smarter or luckier
conditions: Applies to most business and skill domains
claims.mechanism: Most competitors quit at the first sign of real difficulty or uncertainty; the ones who endure long enough to accumulate the necessary mistake-count to solve each level face a self-selecting, shrinking competitor pool at every stage.

numbers.axis: competitive position achievable through persistence alone

anchors.value: top 1% without superior intelligence or luck

examples.text: Before growing Gym Launch and his other businesses, Alex Hormozi operated nine simultaneous businesses: a dental agency, a chiropractic agency, a launch business that required weekly travel to different cities, and six gym locations. Despite generating revenue across all nine, he made no meaningful profit because his attention was too spread to execute effectively on any single business. Looking back, he says the obvious solution was to focus on one — but at the time he believed the problem was his strategy rather than his execution spread.

A solar sales company doing multi-figure revenue held a two-day leadership offsite where their team collectively agreed on six pillars of sales leadership, including accountability, time management, and similar abstract concepts. After the offsite, no one changed their behavior. When Alex Hormozi diagnosed the problem, he pointed out that 'accountability' meant different things to different people. He pressed the founder to describe what someone holding someone accountable actually does — the result was a list of specific observable behaviors: texting the team each morning, conducting end-of-week one-on-one reviews, giving public kudos to high performers, and asking underperformers what they were struggling with. Hormozi's prescription: say those specific behaviors, not the abstract word. The team cannot be held accountable to a word they interpret differently.

Alex Hormozi uses a hiring scenario for a videographer to illustrate the off-hours screening method. If a videographer candidate says their off-hours consist of watching YouTube videos about lighting improvements, audio quality, and set design — that they are genuinely obsessed with video craft — Hormozi treats that as strong positive signal. In contrast, if the candidate says they love pickleball and working out (activities unrelated to the role), Hormozi does not treat that as disqualifying on its own, but notes it means their discretionary effort is flowing toward non-role skills, which will limit their improvement rate and full-time output in the videographer role.

practices.text: Use the Start-Stop-Keep feedback format when diagnosing culture or giving team feedback: specify what you want someone to start doing that they are not doing, stop doing that they are currently doing, and keep doing that is already working. This operationalizes culture critique into actionable behavioral directives.

When diagnosing why a business plan is not being executed, identify whether the root cause is culture (reinforcement rules are wrong), talent (people quality is insufficient), or training (abstract goals have not been converted to observable behaviors) before changing strategy.

During hiring interviews, ask candidates what they do in their off time and what they are obsessed with. Use this to determine whether their discretionary effort flows toward the skill required by the role.

When evaluating abstract leadership or culture terms like 'accountability,' press yourself to describe the observable behaviors that would constitute that term in action — what would a third party see happening? Replace the abstract term in training and feedback with those observable behaviors.

Before switching business strategy, diagnose whether the constraint is cultural, talent-based, or training-based; solve the present constraint on the current path before abandoning it, because switching paths resets accumulated progress to zero.
